en: Vibhaṅga:
Analysis of the Truths 1.
Suttantabhājanīya (The Exposition According to the Discourses)
The Four Noble Truths:
the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
1.1. The Truth of Suffering.
Therein, what is the Noble Truth of Suffering?
Birth is suffering; aging is suffering; death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering;
association with the unpleasant is suffering; separation from the pleasant is suffering; not to obtain what one desires is suffering.
That too is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
Therein, what is birth?
It is the birth, the being born, the descent, the production, the manifestation of the aggregates, and the acquisition of the sense bases of this or that being within this or that class of beings.
This is called "birth.
In that regard, what is "aging"?

It is the aging of those various beings in their respective classes of beings; it is decrepitude, brokenness, graying of hair, wrinkling of skin, the dwindling away of the life-span, and the maturation of the faculties.
This is called "aging.
In this context, what is "death"?

It is the passing away, the vanishing, the breaking up, the disappearance, the mortality, the death, the making of time, the breaking up of the aggregates, the laying down of the body, and the cutting off of the life-faculty of this or that being from this or that class of beings.
This is called "death.
In this context, what is sorrow?
It is the state of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives, or afflicted by the loss of wealth, or afflicted by illness.
For one who is touched by the ruin of virtue, or touched by the ruin of view, or possessed of some other kind of ruin,
or touched by some form of suffering: sorrow, grieving, the state of grieving,
inner sorrow, inner despondency, the burning of the mind, mental distress, and the dart of sorrow.
This is called "sorrow" (śoka).
In this context, what is "lamentation" (parideva)?
It is the state of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives, or afflicted by the loss of wealth, or afflicted by the loss of health.
For one who is afflicted by the ruin of virtue or the ruin of view, or who is possessed of this or that misfortune,
or who is touched by this or that painful state— there is weeping, lamentation, the act of weeping, the act of lamentation,
the state of having wept, the state of having lamented; it is idle chatter, confused chatter, wailing, the act of wailing, the state of having wailed.
This is called lamentation.
In this context, what is suffering?
That which is bodily unpleasantness, bodily pain, the unpleasant and painful feeling born of body-contact, the unpleasant and painful sensation born of body-contact—this is called suffering.
This is called "suffering" (dukkha).
In this context, what is mental grief (domanassa)?
It is that which is mental unease, mental suffering, an unpleasant and painful experience born of mental contact—an unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact.
This is called "mental distress" (*domanassa*).
In this context, what is "despair" (*upāyāsa*)?
It is the state of one who is afflicted by misfortune concerning relatives, or afflicted by misfortune concerning wealth, or afflicted by misfortune concerning illness.
For one who is afflicted by the ruin of virtue, or afflicted by the ruin of view, or possessed of this or that other ruin,
or afflicted by this or that other state of suffering— the striving, the intense striving, the state of having striven, the state of having intensely striven—
this is called "despair" (*upāyāsa*).
In this context, what is the suffering of association with the unpleasant?

Here, there are forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles that are undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable to one; or there are those who wish one no welfare, who wish one harm, who wish one discomfort, and who wish one lack of security from bondage.
Whatever association, meeting, encounter, or mingling there is with them—that is [the suffering of association with the unpleasant].
This is called "association with the unpleasant is suffering.
In this context, what is "separation from the pleasant is suffering"?
Here, whatever forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tactile objects one has that are desired, liked, and agreeable, or whatever else...
They are those who desire one's welfare, who desire one's benefit, who desire one's comfort, and who desire one's security from bondage—
whether they be mother, father, brother, sister, friend, colleague, kinsman, or blood relative.
That which constitutes non-association, non-meeting, non-convergence, and non-mingling with them— [that is what is meant].
This is called “separation from the beloved is suffering.
In this context, what is “not to get what one desires is also suffering”?
For beings subject to birth, such a desire arises: [“O, that we were not subject to birth!”]
“Oh, that we were not subject to birth!
Oh, that birth would not come upon us!
Yet this cannot be attained by mere wishing.
This too is "not to obtain what one desires is suffering.
For beings subject to aging...
[and so on] ...for beings subject to illness... [and so on].
In beings subject to death...
[and so on] ...in beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, such a wish arises:
"O, that we were not subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair!"
"Indeed, may grief, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair not come upon us!
But this cannot be attained by wishing.
This too is "not to get what one wishes for is suffering."
In this regard, what are, in brief, the five aggregates of clinging that are suffering?
They are as follows:

the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to volitional formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
These, in brief, are called "the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
This is called "the noble truth of suffering.
1.2. The Truth of the Origin [of Suffering]
Therein, what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there;
namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
Now, where does this craving arise when arising, and where does it settle when settling?
It arises when arising and settles when settling in whatever in the world is agreeable and pleasurable.
And what in the world is agreeable and pleasurable?
The eye is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
The ear in the world … the nose in the world … [and so on].
The tongue in the world… the body in the world… the mind in the world is a lovely form, a pleasant form; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Forms in the world are dear things, pleasant things; herein this craving, when arising, arises; herein, when settling, it settles.
Sounds in the world...
smells in the world... [and so on].
Tastes in the world...
tangibles in the world...
mental phenomena in the world are dear things, pleasant things; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Eye-consciousness is a lovely thing and a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Ear-consciousness in the world … nose-consciousness in the world … [and so on].
Tongue-consciousness in the world...
body-consciousness in the world...
mind-consciousness in the world is a delightful form, a pleasurable form; herein this craving, when arising, arises; herein, when settling, it settles.
Eye-contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises; herein, when settling, it settles.
Ear-contact in the world... [and so on]...
Nose-contact in the world...
Tongue-contact in the world...
body-contact in the world...
mind-contact in the world is a lovely form, a pleasant form; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Feeling born of eye-contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Feeling born of ear-contact is a lovely thing… feeling born of nose-contact is a lovely thing… [and so on].
Feeling born of tongue-contact in the world...
feeling born of body-contact in the world...
feeling born of mind-contact in the world is a lovely form, a pleasant form; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Perception of forms is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Perception of sounds in the world...
perception of odors in the world... [and so on].
In the world, the perception of tastes... the perception of tangibles...
the perception of mental phenomena is a lovely form, a pleasant form; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Volition regarding forms is a source of endearment and gratification in the world; herein this craving arises when it arises, and herein it settles when it settles.
Volition regarding sounds in the world … volition regarding odors in the world … [and so on].

Volition regarding tastes in the world… volition regarding tangibles in the world… volition regarding mental phenomena in the world is a form that is dear and pleasant; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Craving for forms is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Craving for sounds in the world … craving for odors in the world … [and so on].

Craving for tastes in the world… craving for tangibles in the world… craving for mental phenomena in the world is a form that is dear and pleasant; herein this craving arises when it arises, and herein it settles when it settles.
In the world, thought of forms is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Thought of sounds in the world … thought of odors in the world … [and so on].

In the world, reflection on tastes… reflection on tangibles… reflection on mental phenomena is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when arising, arises; herein, when settling, it settles.
In the world, the investigation of forms is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
In the world, the investigation of sounds is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
In the world, the investigation of odors is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Investigation of tastes is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Investigation of tangibles is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
Investigation of mental phenomena is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when arising, arises, and when settling, settles.
This is called "the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
1.3. The Truth of Cessation:
In this context, what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?
It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishment, its abandonment, its release, and its non-attachment.
Now, where is this craving abandoned when it is being abandoned, and where does it cease when it is ceasing?
It is in regard to whatever in the world is pleasant and agreeable that this craving is abandoned when it is being abandoned, and it ceases when it is ceasing.
And what in the world is of a pleasant nature, of a delightful nature?

The eye in the world is of a pleasant nature, of a delightful nature; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases. The ear in the world … [and so on for the other sense bases] … the mind in the world is of a pleasant nature, of a delightful nature; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases.
The nose in the world...
the tongue in the world...
the body in the world...
In the world, the mind is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases.
In the world, forms are a lovely thing, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases. In the world, sounds... [and so on].
Odors in the world … tastes in the world … tangibles in the world …
Mental phenomena (*dhammā*) in the world are dear and pleasant; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, it ceases.
Eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) in the world is dear and pleasant; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, it ceases.
Ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa*) in the world … [and so on] …
Olfactory consciousness in the world...
gustatory consciousness in the world...
tactile consciousness in the world...
Mental consciousness is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases.
Eye-contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases. Ear-contact is a lovely thing... [and so on].
In the world, nose-contact... tongue-contact...
body-contact... [is impermanent].
Mental contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases.
Feeling born of eye-contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases.
Feeling born of ear-contact is a lovely thing in the world... [and so on].
In the world, feeling born of nose-contact … feeling born of tongue-contact … feeling born of body-contact … [is impermanent].
Feeling born of mind-contact is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, ceasing, it ceases.
Perception of forms in the world… perception of sounds in the world…
Perception of odors in the world… perception of tastes in the world… perception of tangibles in the world…
Perception of mental phenomena is a lovely thing, a pleasant thing in the world; herein this craving, being abandoned, is abandoned, and herein, ceasing, it ceases.
Volitional intention regarding forms in the world… volitional intention regarding sounds in the world…
In the world, there is volition regarding odors;
in the world, there is volition regarding tastes;
in the world, there is volition regarding tangibles.

Volitional intention regarding mental phenomena (*dhammasañcetanā*) is a form of endearment and a form of gratification in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, ceases.
Craving for forms in the world… craving for sounds in the world…
Craving for odors in the world … craving for tastes in the world … craving for tangibles in the world …
Craving for phenomena (*dhammataṇhā*) is dear and pleasant in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, it ceases.
Discursive thought of forms in the world… discursive thought of sounds in the world…
In the world, there is reflection on odors;
in the world, there is reflection on tastes;
in the world, there is reflection on tangibles.
Reflection on mental phenomena (*dhamma-vitakka*) is a form of endearment and gratification in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, ceases.
Discursive thought regarding forms (*rūpa-vicāra*) in the world… discursive thought regarding sounds (*sadda-vicāra*) in the world…
In the world there is the investigation of odors;
in the world there is the investigation of tastes;
in the world there is the investigation of tangibles.
Investigation of phenomena is a state of endearment and gratification in the world; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned, and when ceasing, ceases.
This is called "the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
1.4. The Truth of the Path.
Therein, what is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is this very noble eightfold path; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
In this context, what is right view?
Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—
this is called right view.
In this context, what is right intention?
The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-cruelty—
this is called "right intention."
In this context, what is right speech?
Abstinence from false speech, abstinence from malicious speech, abstinence from harsh speech, and abstinence from idle chatter—
this is called right speech.
In this context, what is right action?
Refraining from taking life, refraining from taking what is not given, and refraining from sexual misconduct—
this is called "right action."
In this context, what is right livelihood?
Here, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, maintains his life by means of right livelihood—
this is called "right livelihood."
In this regard, what is right effort?
Here, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states.
He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states.
One generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen.

One generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have already arisen.
This is called right effort (*sammāvāyāma*).
Therein, what is right mindfulness?
Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
[He dwells] in feelings …pe…

He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind... and he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
This is called "right mindfulness."
In this regard, what is right concentration?

Here, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without applied thought and without sustained thought, and possesses rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
With the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: “He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness. Thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
This is called "right concentration.
This is called "the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
This concludes the Suttantabhājanīya.
2. The Exposition of the Abhidhamma:
The Four Truths—suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this context, what is the origin of suffering?
Craving—
this is called "the origin of suffering."
In this context, what is suffering?
It consists of the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, the three wholesome roots associated with the taints,
the remaining wholesome states associated with the taints, the results of wholesome and unwholesome states associated with the taints, and those states which...
Functional states that are neither wholesome nor unwholesome and are not the result of kamma, as well as all form—
this is called "suffering.
In this context, what is the cessation of suffering?
The abandoning of craving—
this is called the cessation of suffering.
In this context, what is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?

Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads out, which goes toward the abandoning [of defilements], for the attainment of the first stage—being secluded from sensual pleasures...
he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge—at that time there is the eightfold path: right view... right concentration.
Therein, what is right view? That which is wisdom,

understanding … [as above] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view, the factor of enlightenment consisting in the investigation of phenomena, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called "right view."
In this context, what is right intention?
That which is reasoning, thought, ... [as above] ... right intention, a factor of the path, included within the path—this is called "right intention."
In this context, what is right speech?

That which is the refraining from, the abstaining from, the desisting from, the abstinence from, the non-doing, the non-performing, the non-transgression of, and the destruction of the bridge regarding the four kinds of verbal misconduct; that which is right speech, a factor of the path, included within the path—this is called "right speech."
In this context, what is right action?

That which is the refraining, abstaining, desisting, and abstinence from the three types of bodily misconduct; the non-doing, non-performance, non-transgression, non-overstepping of the limit, and the destruction of the bridge [to such conduct]—this is called right action, a factor of the path, included within the path.
In this context, what is right livelihood?

That which is the refraining from, the abstaining from, the desisting from, the abstinence from, the non-performance, the non-doing, the non-transgression of, the not overstepping the limit of, and the destruction of the bridge to wrong livelihood; that which is right livelihood, a factor of the path, included within the path—this is called "right livelihood."
In this context, what is right effort?
That which is the arousal of mental energy … [as before] … right effort, the enlightenment factor of energy, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called "right effort."
In this context, what is right mindfulness?

That which is mindfulness, constant mindfulness... [as before] ...right mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, a factor of the path, included within the path—this is called "right mindfulness."
Therein, what is right concentration?
That stability and steadfastness of the mind … [as above] … right concentration, the factor of enlightenment called concentration, the path factor included in the path—
this is called "right concentration."
This is called "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
All remaining phenomena are associated with the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this context, what is the origin of suffering?
Craving and the remaining defilements—
this is called the "origin of suffering.
In this context, what is suffering?
The remaining unwholesome states; the three wholesome roots associated with the outflows; the remaining wholesome states associated with the outflows;

the results of wholesome and unwholesome states associated with the outflows; those states which are functional, being neither wholesome nor unwholesome and not the result of kamma; and all material form.
This is called "suffering.
In this context, what is the cessation of suffering?
It is the abandoning of craving and of all remaining defilements.
This is called "the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that is emancipating and leads to the destruction [of the defilements], [and which transcends] all views...

For the sake of abandoning [the defilements] and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures …pe… he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time there is the eightfold path:
right view …pe… right concentration.
This is called "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
All remaining phenomena are associated with the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this context, what is the origin of suffering?
Craving and the remaining defilements, as well as the remaining unwholesome states—
this is called "the origin of suffering."
In this context, what is suffering?
It consists of the three wholesome roots associated with the taints, the remaining wholesome states associated with the taints,
the results of wholesome and unwholesome states associated with the taints, those states which are functional— being neither wholesome nor unwholesome nor the result of kamma— and all form.
This is called "suffering.
In this context, what is the cessation of suffering?
It is the abandoning of craving, as well as the remaining defilements and the remaining unwholesome states.
This is called "the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
Here, a bhikkhu, at whatever time he develops supramundane jhāna that is emancipating and leads to the dismantling [of the defilements], [freeing him] from views...

For the sake of abandoning [the hindrances] and for the attainment of the first stage, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time there is the eightfold path:
right view … right concentration.
This is called "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
All remaining phenomena are associated with the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this context, what is the origin of suffering?
Craving, the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, and the three wholesome roots that are subject to taints—
this is called the "origin of suffering.
In this context, what is suffering?

The remaining conditioned phenomena associated with taints that are wholesome; the results of both wholesome and unwholesome phenomena associated with taints; those phenomena which are functional (kiriya), being neither wholesome nor unwholesome and not the result of kamma;
and all form—this is called "suffering.
In this context, what is the cessation of suffering?
The abandoning of craving, of the remaining defilements, of the remaining unwholesome states, and of the three wholesome roots associated with the outflows—
this is called the cessation of suffering.
In this context, what is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?

Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the abandoning of views, and leads to the attainment of the first stage, being secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as above] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge; at that time there is the eightfold path:
Right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
This is called “the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
All remaining phenomena are associated with the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this context, what is the origin of suffering?
It is craving, the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, the three wholesome roots associated with the taints, and the remaining wholesome states associated with the taints—
this is called the origin of suffering.
In this context, what is suffering?
The results of wholesome and unwholesome states that are subject to taints, those states which are functional (neither wholesome nor unwholesome) and are not the result of kamma, and all form—
this is called "suffering."
In this context, what is the cessation of suffering?

It is the abandoning of craving, of the remaining defilements, of the remaining unwholesome states, of the three wholesome roots associated with the taints, and of the remaining wholesome states associated with the taints—
this is called the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?

Here, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna—leading to liberation, leading to the diminution of formations—for the abandoning of views and for the attainment of the first stage, secluded from sensual pleasures... [and so on] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
He dwells in a practice that is painful with sluggish direct knowledge; at that time there is the Eightfold Path—right view ...
pe ... right concentration.
This is called "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
The remaining phenomena are associated with the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
There are four truths:
suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this context, what is the origin of suffering?
Craving—
this is called "the origin of suffering."
In this context, what is suffering?
It consists of the remaining defilements, the remaining unwholesome states, the three wholesome roots that are subject to taints,
the remaining wholesome states that are subject to taints, the results of wholesome and unwholesome states that are subject to taints, and those states which...
Functional states that are neither wholesome nor unwholesome and do not have kamma as their result, and all form—
this is called "suffering.
In this context, what is the cessation of suffering?
The abandoning of craving—
this is called "the cessation of suffering.
In that regard, what is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the waning of existence,
and is for the abandoning of views and the attainment of the first stage— secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...he enters and dwells in the first jhāna,
which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge— at that time there is a five-factored path:
Right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Therein, what is right view?

That which is wisdom, understanding … [as above] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, a factor of the path, included within the path.
This is called right view.
In this context, what is right intention?
That which is reasoning, initial application of the mind... [as above] ...right intention, a factor of the path, included within the path.
This is called "right intention.
In this context, what is right effort?
It is the arousal of mental energy … [as before] … right effort, the factor of enlightenment of energy, a factor of the path, included within the path.
This is called right effort.
In this context, what is right mindfulness?
That which is mindfulness, constant mindfulness... [as above] ...right mindfulness, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, a factor of the path, included within the path.
This is called “right mindfulness.
In this context, what is right concentration?
That stability of the mind … [as above] … right concentration, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, the path factor included in the path.
This is called "right concentration.
This is called "the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

The truth of cessation is without rapture.
Three truths may be with rapture, or they may be without rapture.
The truth of cessation is not accompanied by rapture.
Three truths may be accompanied by rapture, or they may not be accompanied by rapture.
The truth of cessation is not accompanied by pleasure.
Three truths may be accompanied by pleasure, or they may not be accompanied by pleasure.
The truth of cessation is not accompanied by equanimity.
Three truths may be accompanied by equanimity, or they may not be accompanied by equanimity.
The truth of origination belongs to the sense sphere.
Two truths do not belong to the sense sphere.
The truth of suffering may belong to the sense sphere, or it may not belong to the sense sphere.
Three truths are not of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).
The truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) may be of the fine-material sphere, or it may not be of the fine-material sphere.
Three truths are not of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*).
The truth of suffering may be immaterial-sphere (arūpāvacara) or may not be immaterial-sphere.
Two truths are included (pariyāpanna).
Two truths are not included (apariyāpanna).
The truth of the path leads to liberation;
the other three truths do not lead to liberation.
The truth of the path is fixed.
The truth of cessation is indeterminate.
Two truths may be determinate or may be indeterminate.
Two truths are surpassable.
Two truths are unsurpassed.
The truth of the origin is with conflict.
Two truths are without conflict.
The truth of suffering may be with conflict (*saraṇa*) and may be without conflict (*araṇa*). This concludes the interrogation by questions.
The Analysis of the Truths (*Saccavibhaṅga*) is finished.
